**Problem 10 (Challenge): The tax rate that raises the most revenue.** A hypothetical finance minister wants
the labor income tax of Fig. 4 to raise as much revenue as possible. Revenue is the tax on each unit of work
(the green bar) times employment: $\tau\,w'\,L'$.

(a) Set $\tau$ to 0.2, 0.4, 0.6 and 0.8, and compute the revenue from the numbers in the title. Which of the four
rates raises the most?

(b) At employment $L$, firms pay the wage on the demand curve and workers keep the wage on the supply curve.
Show that the tax per unit of work is $(100 - L) - (10 + L) = 90 - 2L$, so that revenue is $(90 - 2L)L$. Find the
employment that maximizes revenue, then the tax rate that produces it. Confirm with a loop over $\tau$ that
uses `equilibrium`.

(c) The country taxes labor at 70 percent. The minister proposes to cut the rate to the value you found in (b).
What happens to revenue and to employment? Why should no government choose a rate above that value?

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

(a) Revenue is (firms pay − workers keep) × $L'$. (b) $(90 - 2L)L$ is an upside-down parabola: set its
derivative to zero ([Appendix C.7](https://quarcs-lab.github.io/macro102-site/notebooks/appC-math-review-for-macroeconomics.html#c.7-derivatives-and-marginal-thinking)).
Then $1 - \tau$ is the wage workers keep divided by the wage firms pay.

</details>

```{python}
#| kind: widget
interact(income_tax,
         tau=FloatSlider(value=0.25, min=0, max=0.8, step=0.05, description="tax rate τ", style=WIDE),
         b_s=fixed(1.0));
```

**Source.** The model of Fig. 4 above, adapted from Fig. 7.4 in Jones (2024), [*Macroeconomics*, 6th ed.](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324063612)

```{python}
# Your answer here
```

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

(a) From the titles: at $\tau = 0.2$, $L' = 38.9$, firms pay 61.1 and workers keep 48.9, so revenue is
$(61.1 - 48.9)\times 38.9 \approx 475$. At 0.4, 0.6 and 0.8 the title numbers give about 861, 1010 and 609
(the loop below gives the exact values). Of the four rates, **60 percent** raises the most. Revenue first rises and then falls with the tax rate: a *Laffer curve*.

```python
for tau in [0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8]:
    L_t, w_t = equilibrium(tau=tau)
    print(f"tau = {tau:.1f}: L' = {L_t:.1f}, revenue = {tau * w_t * L_t:.1f}")
best_tau, best_revenue = 0.0, 0.0
for i in range(90):                                # tau = 0.00, 0.01, ..., 0.89
    tau = i / 100
    L_t, w_t = equilibrium(tau=tau)
    if tau * w_t * L_t > best_revenue:
        best_tau, best_revenue = tau, tau * w_t * L_t
print(f"Highest revenue on the grid: tau = {best_tau:.2f}, revenue = {best_revenue:.1f}")
L_70, w_70 = equilibrium(tau=0.7)
print(f"At tau = 0.70: L' = {L_70:.1f}, revenue = {0.7 * w_70 * L_70:.1f}")
```

The loop prints revenues of 475.3, 859.4, 1010.2 and 611.1, and finds the highest revenue on its grid at
$\tau = 0.58$: 1012.5.

(b) At employment $L$, firms pay $w = 100 - L$ (demand) and workers keep $10 + L$ (supply). The tax per unit of
work is the gap, $90 - 2L$, and revenue is

$$T(L) = (90 - 2L)\,L = 90L - 2L^2, \qquad T'(L) = 90 - 4L = 0 \;\Longrightarrow\; L = 22.5.$$

Revenue is highest when the tax cuts employment to **half** its no-tax level of 45. There, firms pay
$100 - 22.5 = 77.5$ and workers keep $10 + 22.5 = 32.5$, so $1 - \tau = 32.5/77.5 = 0.419$ and
$\tau = 0.581$, or **58.1 percent**. Revenue is $45 \times 22.5 = 1012.5$, as the loop found.

(c) At 70 percent, employment is 15.4 and revenue 911.2. Cutting the rate to 58.1 percent raises revenue to
1012.5, about 11 percent more, **and** employment to 22.5. Above the peak, a lower rate gives more revenue and
more jobs at the same time, so a government there could do better on both counts. Below the peak, a tax cut
costs revenue, and the government has to weigh revenue against jobs.

</details>

percent. A hypothetical free-college program leads 10 more people, at every wage, to work as college graduates

new high school wage and employment with `equilibrium`. The widget cannot show this, because Fig. 9 keeps the
high school market fixed.

in the high school wage?

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

(a) Solved for $L$, the supply curve reads $L = (w - \bar{a}_s)/0.6$. To raise $L$ by 10 at every wage,
$\bar{a}_s$ must fall by $0.6 \times 10 = 6$, so the supply shift grows from 10 to 16. At 16 the title reads

$0.4 \times 6/1 = 2.4$, from 71 to 68.6, and college employment rises by $6/1 = 6$, from 85 to 91: less than 10,
because the lower wage leads some graduates to work less.

(b) and (c):

```python
L_h, w_h = equilibrium(a_s=20.0)                              # high school: supply up by 10

```

(b) The high school wage rises from 55 to **60** and high school employment falls from 45 to 40: with equal
slopes, half of the shift of 10 shows up in the wage.

(c) The premium falls to $68.6/60 - 1 = 0.143$, or **14.3 percent**, from 29.1 percent. The widget's 25 percent, which keeps
the high school wage at 55, misses more than half of the effect. The high school wage rises by 9.1 percent,
while the college wage falls by only 3.4 percent: the rise at the bottom narrows the gap more.

(d) Technology keeps shifting the demand for college graduates out, which widens the premium. Education shifts
the supply of college graduates out and the supply of high school graduates back, which narrows the premium from
both sides. Whichever moves faster wins the race. Goldin and Katz argue that fast growth in the supply of skills
narrowed wage gaps from 1915 to 1980, and that its slowdown after 1980 is a major reason the college premium rose.
